claim: DUX4 was recently characterized as a suppressor of interferon-γ signaling and antigen presentation that is aberrantly expressed in a small subset of primary tumors.
source: The embryonic transcription factor DUX4 was recently characterized as a suppressor of interferon-γ signaling and antigen presentation that is aberrantly expressed in a small subset of primary tumors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Chew et al., 2019; Spens et al., 2023) mentioned later in the manuscript.

claim: DUX4 expression is a common feature of metastatic tumors, with ~10–50% of advanced bladder, breast, kidney, prostate, and skin cancers expressing DUX4.
source: Here, we report that DUX4 expression is a common feature of metastatic tumors, with ~10–50% of advanced bladder, breast, kidney, prostate, and skin cancers expressing DUX4.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1B showing the proportion of DUX4-expressing cancers in metastatic cohorts.

claim: DUX4 expression is significantly associated with immune cell exclusion in urothelial carcinoma patients.
source: DUX4 expression is significantly associated with immune cell exclusion and decreased objective response to PD-L1 blockade in a large cohort of urothelial carcinoma patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing immune phenotypes (Figure 2F) and gene expression signatures (Figure 2C).

claim: DUX4 expression is significantly associated with decreased objective response to PD-L1 blockade in urothelial carcinoma patients.
source: DUX4 expression is significantly associated with immune cell exclusion and decreased objective response to PD-L1 blockade in a large cohort of urothelial carcinoma patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by RECIST response data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: DUX4 expression is a significant predictor of survival even after accounting for tumor mutational burden and other molecular and clinical features in urothelial carcinoma patients.
source: DUX4 expression is a significant predictor of survival even after accounting for tumor mutational burden and other molecular and clinical features in this cohort, with DUX4 expression associated with a median reduction in survival of over 1 year.
evidence: This claim is supported by multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression analysis shown in Figure 4A and Random Survival Forest modeling in Figure 5.

claim: DUX4 expression is associated with a median reduction in survival of over 1 year in urothelial carcinoma patients treated with PD-L1 blockade.
source: DUX4 expression is a significant predictor of survival even after accounting for tumor mutational burden and other molecular and clinical features in this cohort, with DUX4 expression associated with a median reduction in survival of over 1 year.
evidence: This claim is supported by the partial dependence analysis shown in Figure 5F, which measures a difference of at least 12.5 months in median survival between DUX4+ and DUX4− strata.

claim: Blockade of T cell co-inhibitory receptors, such as CTLA-4 and the PD-1/PD-L1 axis, has achieved major success in the treatment of diverse metastatic cancers compared to first-line chemotherapy.
source: Blockade of T cell co-inhibitory receptors, such as CTLA-4 and the PD-1/PD-L1 axis, has achieved major success in the treatment of diverse metastatic cancers compared to first-line chemotherapy (Doki et al., 2022; Hellmann et al., 2019; Klein et al., 2020; Larkin et al., 2019; Motzer et al., 2020; Stein et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: A majority of advanced cancer patients fail to respond to ICI due to de novo or acquired resistance.
source: However, a majority of advanced cancer patients fail to respond to ICI due to de novo or acquired resistance, the mechanistic bases of which remain incompletely understood.
evidence: This claim is based on established clinical knowledge about ICI response rates.

claim: Defects in Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) class I-mediated antigen presentation due to loss of B2M or HLA contribute to ICI resistance.
source: These mechanisms include defects in Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) class I-mediated antigen presentation due to loss of B2M or HLA (Grasso et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2020; McGranahan et al., 2016; Sade-Feldman et al., 2017; Sucker et al., 2014; Wolf et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: PTEN and LSD1 inactivation sensitizes tumor cells to type I interferon signaling.
source: PTEN and LSD1 inactivation, which sensitizes tumor cells to type I interferon signaling (Li et al., 2016; Peng et al., 2016; Sheng et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Active WNT–β-catenin signaling contributes to ICI resistance.
source: and active WNT–β-catenin signaling (Spranger et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Tumor cell-intrinsic interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) signaling is particularly important in anti-tumor immunity.
source: Tumor cell-intrinsic interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) signaling is particularly important in anti-tumor immunity.
evidence: This claim is based on established immunological knowledge and is supported by subsequent citations.

claim: IFN-γ signaling induces expression of genes involved in MHC class I-mediated antigen processing and presentation, including TAP1/TAP2 transporters, immunoproteasome components, HLA proteins, and B2M.
source: This pathway induces expression of genes involved in MHC class I-mediated antigen processing and presentation, which include genes encoding the TAP1/TAP2 transporters, components of the immunoproteasome, HLA proteins, and B2M (Alspach et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Suppression of IFN-γ activity promotes tumor immune evasion and decreased CD8+ T cell activation.
source: Thus, suppression of IFN-γ activity promotes tumor immune evasion and decreased CD8+ T cell activation.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference from the role of IFN-γ in antigen presentation.

claim: Decreased ICI efficacy was observed in patients with tumors harboring inactivating mutations in IFN-γ pathway genes such as JAK1 and JAK2.
source: Indeed, decreased ICI efficacy was observed in patients with tumors harboring inactivating mutations in IFN-γ pathway genes such as JAK1 and JAK2 (Gao et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2021; Sucker et al., 2017; Zaretsky et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple clinical studies.

claim: A splicing-augmenting mutation in JAK3, linked to decreased JAK3 expression levels, was reported as a potential mechanism of resistance in a patient with metastatic melanoma treated with anti-PD-1 and anti-CTLA-4 combination therapy.
source: Similarly, a recent study reported a splicing-augmenting mutation in JAK3, linked to decreased JAK3 expression levels, as a potential mechanism of resistance in a patient with metastatic melanoma treated with anti-PD-1 and anti-CTLA-4 combination therapy (Newell et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: DUXB is expressed in diverse primary malignancies, most notably in testicular germ cell and breast carcinomas.
source: For instance, DUXB is expressed in diverse primary malignancies, most notably in testicular germ cell and breast carcinomas (Preussner et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: DUX4 is expressed in a small subset of primary tumors, where it suppresses tumor cell antigen presentation and response to IFN-γ signaling.
source: Recent work from our group and others showed that DUX4 is expressed in a small subset of primary tumors, where it suppresses tumor cell antigen presentation and response to IFN-γ signaling (Chew et al., 2019; Spens et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: DUX4 expression was associated with reduced survival following response to anti-CTLA-4 or anti-PD-1 in melanoma in two small cohorts (n = 27 or 41 patients).
source: We additionally observed signals that DUX4 expression was associated with reduced survival following response to anti-CTLA-4 or anti-PD-1 in melanoma; however, those analyses relied upon two small cohorts (n = 27 or 41 patients), limiting the statistical power of our conclusions.
evidence: This claim is based on prior work by the authors with limited statistical power.

claim: DUX4 initializes human zygotic genome activation in its native embryonic context.
source: In its native embryonic context, DUX4 initializes human zygotic genome activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies on DUX4 function in embryos.

claim: DUX4 expression levels peak at the 4-cell stage of the cleavage embryo.
source: DUX4 expression levels peak at the 4-cell stage of the cleavage embryo; DUX4 is then immediately silenced via epigenetic repression of the D4Z4 repeat array that contains the DUX4 gene (De Iaco et al., 2017; Hendrickson et al., 2017; Himeda and Jones, 2019; Sugie et al., 2020; Whiddon et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on embryonic DUX4 expression.

claim: DUX4 is silenced via epigenetic repression of the D4Z4 repeat array that contains the DUX4 gene after the 4-cell stage.
source: DUX4 expression levels peak at the 4-cell stage of the cleavage embryo; DUX4 is then immediately silenced via epigenetic repression of the D4Z4 repeat array that contains the DUX4 gene (De Iaco et al., 2017; Hendrickson et al., 2017; Himeda and Jones, 2019; Sugie et al., 2020; Whiddon et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on DUX4 silencing mechanisms.

claim: DUX4 remains silenced in adult somatic tissues aside from select sites of immune privilege such as the testis.
source: Aside from select sites of immune privilege such as the testis, DUX4 remains silenced in adult somatic tissues (Das and Chadwick, 2016; Snider et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: DUX4 expression in cancer cells suppresses MHC class I-mediated antigen presentation.
source: Since DUX4 expression in cancer cells suppresses MHC class I-mediated antigen presentation (Chew et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: A markedly higher proportion of advanced metastatic cancers express DUX4 compared to their TCGA cancer counterparts.
source: A markedly higher proportion of advanced metastatic cancers express DUX4—and tend to have higher absolute DUX4 expression levels—than do their TCGA cancer counterparts (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and 1C comparing DUX4 expression in TCGA vs. metastatic cohorts.

claim: Advanced metastatic cancers tend to have higher absolute DUX4 expression levels than their TCGA cancer counterparts.
source: A markedly higher proportion of advanced metastatic cancers express DUX4—and tend to have higher absolute DUX4 expression levels—than do their TCGA cancer counterparts (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C comparing DUX4 expression levels.

claim: DUX4-positive metastatic tumors transcribe the full-length coding region, resembling the cleavage stage embryo and DUX4-expressing primary cancers.
source: Resembling the cleavage stage embryo and DUX4-expressing primary cancers, DUX4-positive metastatic tumors transcribe the full-length coding region.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq coverage data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: B-cell ALL exhibits a C-terminal truncation of DUX4 due to DUX4 fusion with the IGH locus.
source: In contrast, B-cell ALL exhibited the expected C-terminal truncation due to DUX4 fusion with the IGH locus (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq coverage data shown in Figure 1D and is consistent with prior knowledge about DUX4-IGH fusions in B-cell ALL.

claim: DUX4 expression is readily detectable and quantifiable for both poly(A)-selection and hybrid probe capture sequencing library preparations.
source: Our re-analysis revealed that DUX4 expression is readily detectable and quantifiable for both sample and library preparation methods.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C comparing the two methods.

claim: DUX4 transcript levels in the majority of sequenced samples were higher in poly(A)-selected sequencing than in hybrid capture.
source: DUX4 transcript levels in the majority of the sequenced samples were higher in poly(A)-selected sequencing than were the analogous measurements obtained from hybrid capture (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: The high rates of DUX4 expression observed across metastatic cancer cohorts reflect true DUX4 expression rather than technical biases introduced by studying formalin-fixed tissues.
source: These data demonstrate that the high rates of DUX4 expression that we observed across metastatic cancer cohorts reflect true DUX4 expression rather than technical biases introduced by studying formalin-fixed tissues and are consistent with expression of a polyadenylated DUX4 transcript in both primary and metastatic cancers.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the comparison of poly(A) and hybrid capture methods shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: 54% of urothelial cancer patients express DUX4.
source: First, urothelial cancers exhibited one of the highest frequencies of DUX4 expression (54% of patients) in any of the five metastatic cancer cohorts that we analyzed
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis of the urothelial cancer cohort.

claim: Pretreatment samples from 347 patients enrolled in the IMvigor210 trial were subject to transcriptome profiling by RNA-seq as well as immunohistochemical analysis.
source: Second, pretreatment samples from 347 patients enrolled in the IMvigor210 trial, a phase 2 trial of anti-PD-L1 (atezolizumab) therapy with advanced urothelial carcinoma, were subject to transcriptome profiling by RNA-seq as well as immunohistochemical analysis, enabling us to conduct comprehensive studies of the association between DUX4 expression, the global transcriptome, and immunophenotypes in a well-powered cohort (Balar et al., 2017; Mariathasan et al., 2018; Rosenberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the IMvigor210 trial publications.

claim: Gene Ontology network analyses on upregulated genes in DUX4-positive cancers identified multiple clusters of development-associated terms.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) network analyses on the upregulated genes in DUX4-positive cancers identified multiple clusters of development-associated terms, consistent with the known role of DUX4 in early embryogenesis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; De Iaco et al., 2017; Hendrickson et al., 2017; Sugie et al., 2020; Whiddon et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and citations to prior work on DUX4 in embryogenesis.

claim: Downregulated genes in DUX4-positive cancers are associated with GO terms corresponding to humoral or cell-mediated immunity.
source: In contrast, we found a single network associated with downregulated genes: GO terms corresponding to humoral or cell-mediated immunity (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: DUX4-expressing cancers have statistically lower levels of IFN-γ activity.
source: Using an IFN-γ gene signature predictive of response to blockade of the PD-1/PD-L1 axis, we found that DUX4-expressing cancers have statistically lower levels of IFN-γ activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; Ayers et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene signature analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and citation to the signature source.

claim: DUX4 expression is correlated with extensive downregulation of genes involved in MHC class I-dependent antigen presentation and T cell activation.
source: Consistent with IFN-γ suppression, we observed extensive downregulation of genes involved in anti-tumor immunity such as those involved in MHC class I-dependent antigen presentation and T cell activation, checkpoint proteins, and chemokines involved in effector T cell recruitment.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: DUX4 expression is correlated with suppression of genes critical for MHC class II-mediated antigen presentation, including MHC class II isotypes (HLA–DP/DQ/DR), HLA-DM, HLA-DO, and CD74.
source: DUX4-expression was also correlated with suppression of genes critical for MHC class II-mediated antigen presentation, namely: MHC class II isotypes (HLA–DP/DQ/DR), HLA-DM, and HLA-DO, and the invariant chain (CD74) (Roche and Furuta, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2B and citation to prior work on MHC class II.

claim: CIITA is induced by IFN-γ and is downregulated in DUX4-expressing tumors.
source: CIITA is induced by IFN-γ and is also conspicuously downregulated in DUX4-expressing tumors (Figure 2B; Glimcher and Kara, 1992; Masternak et al., 2000; Steimle et al., 1993; Steimle et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2B and citations to prior work on CIITA regulation.

claim: MHC class II-mediated antigen presentation can regulate T cell abundance in the tumor microenvironment and patient response to PD-1 blockade.
source: MHC class II-mediated antigen presentation can regulate T cell abundance in the tumor microenvironment and patient response to PD-1 blockade (Johnson et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: DUX4-expressing cancers had lower measures of the effector CD8+ T cell gene signature, consistent with decreased CD8+ T cell infiltration into the tumor.
source: DUX4-expressing cancers had lower measures of the gene signature, consistent with decreased CD8+ T cell infiltration into the tumor (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene signature analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: DUX4 expression is associated with patterns consistent with widespread immune cell exclusion from the tumor microenvironment.
source: In addition, we observed patterns consistent with widespread immune cell exclusion from the tumor microenvironment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immune cell signature analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: In DUX4-expressing cancers, lower mRNA levels of CXCL9 and CXCL10 were observed.
source: In DUX4-expressing cancers, we observed lower mRNA levels of CXCL9 and CXCL10, chemokines which recruit T cells to the tumor site (Figure 2D,E; Nagarsheth et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2D,E and citation to prior work on chemokine function.

claim: DUX4 expression was correlated with broad reduction in the expression of chemokine signaling genes.
source: Utilizing a chemokine signature associated with host immune response to solid tumors, we observed that DUX4 expression was correlated with broad reduction in the expression of chemokine signaling genes, beyond T cell-associated signals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E; Coppola et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by chemokine signature analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and citation to the signature source.

claim: DUX4 expression in advanced urothelial carcinoma tumors was associated with an immune exclusion phenotype: a higher proportion of DUX4+ tumors exhibit either an immune-excluded or immune-desert phenotype compared to malignancies where DUX4 is silent.
source: We verified that DUX4 expression in the advanced urothelial carcinoma tumors was associated with an immune exclusion phenotype: a higher proportion of DUX4+ tumors exhibit either an immune-excluded or immune-desert phenotype compared to malignancies where DUX4 is silent (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: DUX4 expression was associated with a significant decrease in PD-L1 levels on both tumor and host immune cells.
source: We determined that DUX4 expression was associated with a significant decrease in PD-L1 levels on both tumor and host immune cells, consistent with DUX4-induced suppression of IFN-γ signaling (Figure 2G,H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2G,H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G,H.

claim: PD-L1 expression on immune cells such as dendritic cells and macrophages modulate anti-tumor immune suppression and response to ICI in in vivo mouse models.
source: PD-L1 expression on immune cells such as dendritic cells and macrophages modulate anti-tumor immune suppression and response to ICI in in vivo mouse models (Lau et al., 2017; Lin et al., 2018; Noguchi et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: PD-L1 levels on immune cells are correlated with response to ICI in clinical trials.
source: Importantly, PD-L1 levels on immune cells are correlated with response to ICI in clinical trials (Powles et al., 2014; Rosenberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical trial publications.

claim: DUX4 expression was associated with a significant decrease in objective response rates, assessed using RECIST.
source: DUX4 expression was associated with a significant decrease in objective response rates, assessed using the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical response data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Higher tumor mutational burden (TMB) was linked to improved survival outcomes in the urothelial carcinoma cohort.
source: As expected, higher tumor mutational burden (TMB) was linked to improved survival outcomes in this cohort (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: DUX4 expression was correlated with statistically lower survival rates after crudely adjusting for the effects of TMB by removing the bottom quartile of patients.
source: Interestingly, we found that DUX4 expression was correlated with statistically lower survival rates in this cohort after crudely adjusting for the effects of TMB by removing the bottom quartile of patients, those with the lowest number of missense mutations in their tumors (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In multivariate Cox PH regression, TMB was positively associated with survival (hazard ratio = 0.14).
source: In the context of multivariate Cox PH regression, which controls for the confounding effects of all other covariates simultaneously, we observed that TMB was positively associated with survival [hazard ratio (HR) = 0.14], as expected.
evidence: This claim is supported by Cox regression analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: DUX4 positivity was associated with a 3.2-fold increase in risk of death at any point in time compared to DUX4-negative status in multivariate Cox PH regression.
source: In particular, DUX4 positivity was associated with dramatically worse survival, with a 3.2-fold increase in risk of death at any point in time compared to DUX4-negative status (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 1, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by multivariate Cox regression analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ECOG PS >0 and previous administration of platinum chemotherapy were correlated with increased risk (or shorter survival) in multivariate Cox PH regression.
source: Conversely, DUX4 expression, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group Performance Status (ECOG PS) >0, and previous administration of platinum chemotherapy were correlated with increased risk (or shorter survival)
evidence: This claim is supported by multivariate Cox regression analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: TGFB1 expression did not remain significant after controlling for TMB and other variables in multivariate Cox PH regression.
source: while other features that have previously been reported as associated with reduced survival e.g., TGFB1 expression (Mariathasan et al., 2018) did not remain significant after controlling for TMB and other variables.
evidence: This claim is supported by multivariate Cox regression analysis shown in Figure 4A and citation to prior work.

claim: The addition of DUX4 expression status improves goodness-of-fit measurements in Cox PH models.
source: In these analyses, we observed a quantifiable improvement in data-model congruence with the addition of DUX4 expression status (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by BIC, AIC, and C-index measurements shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: DUX4 expression status is an informative predictor of risk under ICI treatment.
source: Taken together, these analyses indicate that DUX4 expression status is an informative predictor of risk under ICI treatment.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the goodness-of-fit and likelihood ratio test results.

claim: The full Cox PH model (including DUX4 expression status) stratifies patients in an informative manner, appropriately discriminating patients with longer vs. shorter survival times.
source: By empirically quantifying survival of the two risk groups using KM (Kaplan–Meier) estimation, we found that the full model stratifies patients in an informative manner, appropriately discriminating patients with longer vs. shorter survival times (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival curves shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: The addition of DUX4 expression status improves model performance as illustrated by the time-dependent Brier score.
source: Furthermore, the addition of DUX4 expression status improves model performance as illustrated by the time-dependent Brier score, a measure of survival prediction accuracy at specific timepoints (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Brier score analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The RSF model had an out-of-bag (OOB) error of 38.4%.
source: We randomly selected 70% of the patients to grow the forest, with the resulting model having an out-of-bag (OOB) error of 38.4%.
evidence: This claim is based on the RSF model training results.

claim: The RSF model recorded a test error of 32.6%.
source: Thus, we measured the RSF model's test error using a holdout set (the remaining 30% of the cohort) excluded from training. The RSF model recorded a test error of 32.6% illustrating an appropriate fit (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by error measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The RSF model predicted worse survival outcomes in patients with DUX4-expressing cancers compared to their DUX4-silent counterparts.
source: The RSF model predicted worse survival outcomes in patients with DUX4-expressing cancers compared to their DUX4-silent counterparts. These predictions were mirrored in the test dataset, illustrating robustness of the model (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RSF survival predictions shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The RSF model predicted an approximately 20% decrease in both 1- and 1.5-year survival probabilities in patients with DUX4-expressing cancers.
source: Examining the absolute effects of DUX4 expression on survival, the RSF model predicted an approximately 20% decrease in both 1- and 1.5-year survival probabilities in patients with DUX4-expressing cancers (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RSF survival probability predictions shown in Figure 5B.

claim: RSF survival predictions conform closely with the empirical survival estimates obtained via the Kaplan–Meier model.
source: Importantly, RSF survival predictions conform closely with the empirical survival estimates obtained via the Kaplan–Meier model (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of RSF and Kaplan-Meier predictions shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In Shapley value analyses of the RSF model, ECOG PS had the largest contribution to mortality prediction, followed by TMB and DUX4 expression.
source: We estimated Shapley values associated with predicting ensemble mortality, the RSF risk estimate. In these analyses, ECOG PS had the largest contribution, followed by TMB and DUX4 expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Shapley value analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Feature contributions measured using permutation importance and minimal depth were consistent with the Shapley-based assignments, identifying DUX4 expression as an important contributor to patient survival outcomes.
source: Feature contributions measured using permutation importance and minimal depth were consistent with the Shapley-based assignments, notably identifying DUX4 expression as an important contributor to patient survival outcomes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by permutation importance and minimal depth analyses shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The importance of DUX4 expression for survival prediction is most prominent at later times in time-dependent Shapley value analyses.
source: Interestingly, we observed the strong dependence on ECOG PS for predicting survival at early timepoints under this paradigm. The importance of DUX4 expression for survival prediction is most prominent at later times (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-dependent Shapley value analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Comparison of patients with the lowest vs. highest TMB revealed an approximately 67% difference in mortality in partial dependence analysis.
source: Comparison of the patients with the lowest vs. highest TMB revealed an approximately 67% difference in mortality.
evidence: This claim is supported by partial dependence analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: An approximately 53% increase in mortality was measured associated with DUX4 positivity in partial dependence analysis.
source: On the other hand, we measured an approximately 53% increase in mortality associated with DUX4 positivity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by partial dependence analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1I.

claim: DUX4 expression was correlated with a 1- and 1.5-year survival difference of 20.7% and 19.2% between patients with DUX4+ and DUX4− tumors, respectively, in partial dependence analysis.
source: DUX4 expression was correlated with poorer survival outcomes, with a 1- and 1.5-year survival difference of 20.7% and 19.2% between patients with DUX4+ and DUX4− tumors, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by partial dependence analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: A difference of at least 12.5 months in median survival was measured between the DUX4+ and DUX4− strata in partial dependence analysis.
source: Strikingly, our analyses measure a difference of at least 12.5 months in median survival between the DUX4+ and DUX4− strata (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by partial dependence analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: DUX4 expression in the metastatic context is associated with reduced anti-tumor immunity, mirroring previous observations in primary cancers and cancer cell line models.
source: While the mechanism governing DUX4 de-repression in cancer remains to be elucidated, we show that DUX4 expression in the metastatic context is associated with reduced anti-tumor immunity, mirroring previous observations in primary cancers and cancer cell line models (Chew et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by the gene expression and immunophenotype analyses presented in the manuscript and citation to prior work.

claim: DUX4 expression is correlated with decreased patient survival under ICI treatment.
source: and is correlated with decreased patient survival under ICI treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analyses shown in Figures 3-5.

claim: The prognostic value of IFN-γ activity and its non-redundancy relative to TMB in terms of influencing ICI response is widely appreciated.
source: The prognostic value of IFN-γ activity (Ayers et al., 2017; Grasso et al., 2020; Newell et al., 2022) and its non-redundancy relative to TMB in terms of influencing ICI response is widely appreciated (Cristescu et al., 2018; Newell et al., 2022; Rozeman et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: Patients with advanced melanoma that is nonresponsive to anti-CTLA-4 or anti-PD-1/PD-L1 therapy have higher frequencies of genetic alterations associated with IFN-γ signaling defects compared to responsive patients.
source: For example, patients with advanced melanoma that is nonresponsive to anti-CTLA-4 or anti-PD-1/PD-L1 therapy have higher frequencies of genetic alterations associated with IFN-γ signaling defects compared to responsive patients (Gao et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2021; Sucker et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: DUX4 has been implicated in modifying IFN-γ activity through direct binding and inhibition of STAT1 via its C-terminal domain.
source: DUX4 has been implicated in modifying IFN-γ activity through direct binding and inhibition of STAT1 via its C-terminal domain (Chew et al., 2019; Spens et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior mechanistic studies.

claim: DUX4 transcripts in the metastatic context contain the full-length coding region, suggestive of an intact capability as a STAT1 suppressor.
source: Our sequence analyses show that DUX4 transcripts in the metastatic context contain the full-length coding region, suggestive of an intact capability as a STAT1 suppressor.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the RNA-seq coverage data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The contribution of DUX4 expression to survival prediction is most prominent at later timepoints, suggesting principal effects on long-term survival.
source: For instance, the contribution of DUX4 expression to survival prediction is most prominent at later timepoints, suggesting principal effects on long-term survival.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the time-dependent Shapley value analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: ECOG PS negatively impacts patient survival during ICI therapy.
source: ECOG PS negatively impacts patient survival during ICI therapy, inferred from our multivariate Cox PH analysis and from findings of the IMvigor210 clinical trial: patients with ECOG PS = 2 (n = 24) had a median overall survival of 8.1 months, lower than the subgroup with ECOG PS <2 (n = 35) whose median survival was not reached during the observation period (Balar et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by Cox PH analysis results and citation to the IMvigor210 trial.

claim: Other studies have reported poorer outcomes associated with ICI treatment in patients with high ECOG PS.
source: Other studies have similarly reported poorer outcomes associated with ICI treatment in patients with high ECOG PS (Chalker et al., 2022; Krishnan et al., 2022; Cristescu et al., 2018; Sehgal et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: DUX4 expression may promote patient resistance to anti-CTLA-4 and anti-PD-1 therapies.
source: Our previous work showed that DUX4 expression is associated with resistance to anti-CTLA-4 and anti-PD-1 therapies (Chew et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: DUX4 expression in metastasis is correlated with downregulation of TIGIT and other immune checkpoints whose interception are currently under clinical investigation: HAVCR2/TIM3 and LAG3.
source: We also report that DUX4 expression in metastasis is correlated with downregulation of TIGIT (Zhang et al., 2018) and other immune checkpoints whose interception are currently under clinical investigation: HAVCR2/TIM3 (NCT02608268; Dixon et al., 2021) and LAG3 (NCT02658981; Amaria et al., 2022; Tawbi et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression analysis (Figure 2B) and citations to prior work and clinical trials.

claim: Binary categorization of patients according to DUX4 expression status was sufficient to stratify patients according to ICI response.
source: We show that binary categorization of patients according to DUX4 expression status was sufficient to stratify patients according to ICI response.
evidence: This claim is supported by the survival analyses and risk modeling shown in Figures 3-5.

claim: Screening for DUX4 tumor expression, with binarized results such as through IHC using anti-DUX4 antibodies, could have clinical utility.
source: Screening for DUX4 tumor expression, with binarized results such as through IHC using anti-DUX4 antibodies, could have clinical utility.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observed association between DUX4 expression and ICI response.

claim: Endogenous expression of DUX4 during early embryogenesis ranges from approximately 2 to 10 TPM.
source: Endogenous expression of DUX4 during early embryogenesis range from approximately 2 to 10 TPM (Chew et al., 2019; Hendrickson et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies on embryonic DUX4 expression.

claim: DUX4-positive samples are defined as those with expression levels >1 TPM.
source: We have therefore defined DUX4-positive samples as those with expression levels >1 TPM.
evidence: This is a methodological definition used in the study.

claim: For Cox PH and RSF analyses, DUX4-negative samples were defined as those with DUX4 expression levels <0.25 TPM.
source: For these and subsequent analyses, we elected to define DUX4-negative samples as those with DUX4 expression levels <0.25 TPM.
evidence: This is a methodological definition used in the study to avoid misclassifications at very low expression levels.

claim: This scheme excludes 126 patients but presumably produces more reliable categorizations, avoiding potential misclassifications due to loss of sensitivity of bulk RNA-seq at very low expression levels.
source: This scheme excludes 126 patients but presumably produces more reliable categorizations, avoiding potential misclassifications due to loss of sensitivity of bulk RNA-seq at very low expression levels (Mortazavi et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is based on inference about RNA-seq sensitivity and citation to a prior study on RNA-seq quantification.
